summary.text: An ice cap climate, coded EF in the Köppen system, is a polar climate where no month has a mean temperature above 0 °C.
Because it never gets warmer than ice's melting point, snow and ice pile up for good and form large ice sheets, leaving no vegetation.
Its two major areas are Antarctica and Greenland, and it also covers some far-northern islands and the tops of many high mountains.

facts.label: Human presence
facts.value: No civilian communities, some research stations

items.prompt: A high Arctic site's warmest month averages −2 °C. What do you expect on the ground there year after year?

options.label: A short burst of summer wildflowers
Snow that fully melts every July
Ice that keeps building into a sheet
Bare soil swept clear by strong winds

items.explain: When temperatures never pass ice's melting point, accumulated snow and ice remain permanently and over time form a large ice sheet.

items.prompt: Why does tundra have plants while an ice cap climate has none?

options.label: Tundra summers melt the winter ice cover
Tundra soil holds far more salt
Tundra gets sunlight all year round
Tundra lies much closer to the equator

items.explain: Tundra has months above freezing that melt the winter ice, so ice sheets cannot form and vegetation can grow.

items.prompt: Ice cap climates get almost no precipitation. Why is snowfall usually so scarce there?

options.label: Strong sunlight melts snow before it lands
The air is usually too cold to make snow
Ocean winds carry all the clouds away
Thick ice blocks the clouds from forming

items.explain: It is never warm enough for rain and usually too cold to generate snow, so precipitation is nearly non-existent.

items.prompt: If a thick ice sheet suddenly vanished, what would the land underneath do?

options.label: Sink further below the sea
Crack apart into islands
Stay exactly where it is
Rise back upward

items.explain: The ice's weight pushes the land down; removing it lets the land rise again, an effect called post-glacial rebound.

items.prompt: Greenland has an ice cap climate, yet such climates are far rarer on northern land than in Antarctica. What mainly prevents Antarctica-like cold in the far north?

options.label: The Arctic Ocean moderates nearby land
Arctic land gets more hours of sun
Warm volcanoes heat the northern land
Mountains block the coldest northern winds

items.explain: The Arctic Ocean moderates the temperatures of the surrounding land, making Antarctic-level cold impossible there.

items.prompt: Ice sheets slowly flow off the land into the surrounding sea. How do they avoid simply shrinking away?

options.label: Meltwater refreezes on top every night
Sea ice is pushed back onto the land
New snow and ice replace what is lost
Their edges are anchored by frozen rock

items.explain: Ice sheets slowly move off the continents into surrounding waters, and new snow and ice accumulation replaces the lost ice.

paragraphs.heading: What an ice cap climate is
paragraphs.text: In an ice cap climate, a type of polar climate, no month has a mean temperature above 0 °C. In the Köppen climate classification it is written EF. It covers polar regions between 60° and 90° of latitude, including Antarctica and a few of the most northerly Canadian and Russian islands, as well as high ground including the tops of many tall mountains. These areas are normally under a permanent layer of ice and have no plant life.

paragraphs.heading: Why the ice stays
paragraphs.text: Because the temperature never climbs past the point where ice melts, whatever snow and ice collects stays put, and over time it builds into a large ice sheet. The tundra climate, coded ET, is different. Tundra has a summer with temperatures above freezing for several months, which is enough to melt the winter's ice and stop a sheet from forming. That is why tundra has plants and an ice cap does not.

paragraphs.heading: Moving ice, very little snow
paragraphs.text: The ice sheets are not still: they creep slowly off the land into the surrounding seas. Fresh snow and ice then build up to replace what was lost. Yet precipitation in these places is close to zero, since it is never warm enough to rain and usually too cold for snow to form. Some snow arrives anyway, blown onto the sheets by wind from nearby tundra.

paragraphs.heading: Antarctica against the Arctic
paragraphs.text: Antarctica sits over the South Pole with the Southern Ocean all around it, and fast winds circling the continent keep warmer air from temperate zones out. Cut off like this, it has extreme cold found nowhere else, and weather systems rarely push inside. In the north, the Arctic Ocean softens the temperature of nearby land, so ice cap climates are far less common there. Greenland is the only large landmass up there with this climate. The coldest northern winters actually come in subarctic Siberia, at places such as Verkhoyansk, far inland from the ocean.

paragraphs.heading: Land pushed down by ice
paragraphs.text: Ice sheets are often miles thick. Much of the land beneath them lies below sea level, pressed down by the sheer weight of the ice, and would sit under the sea without its ice. Take the ice away and that land would rise back up, an effect called post-glacial rebound.

paragraphs.heading: A feature of icehouse times
paragraphs.text: Ice cap climates appear only during icehouse Earth periods, and there have been five of them in the planet's past. Between those periods, Earth seems to have had no ice even near the poles. What tips the planet into an icehouse includes changes to the atmosphere, how the continents are arranged, and how much energy arrives from the Sun. Earth is in an icehouse period today.
